content: Cellular adaptation refers to the changes that cells undergo in response to adverse environmental conditions. These changes can be either physiological (normal) or pathological (abnormal). There are five primary types of cellular adaptation: atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, dysplasia, and metaplasia. Atrophy is characterized by a reduction in cell size. When a significant number of cells in an organ undergo atrophy, the entire organ decreases in size. A physiological example of atrophy is the reduction in the size of the thymus during early human development, such as in childhood. In contrast, a pathological example is skeletal muscle atrophy, which occurs due to disuse, often referred to as disuse atrophy. Organs and tissues particularly vulnerable to atrophy include skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, secondary sex organs, and the brain. Hypertrophy involves an increase in cell size. When enough cells in an organ undergo hypertrophy, the entire organ enlarges. Organs such as the heart and kidneys are especially prone to hypertrophy. This process is associated with an increase in intracellular proteins rather than the cytosol (the fluid within the cell). Hypertrophy can be triggered by mechanical signals, such as stretching, or trophic signals, such as growth factors. A physiological example of hypertrophy is the enlargement of skeletal muscle in response to sustained weight-bearing exercise. A pathological example is the hypertrophy of cardiac muscle due to hypertension. Hyperplasia refers to an increase in the number of cells, which occurs as a result of increased cell division (mitosis). Physiological hyperplasia can be classified into two types: compensatory and hormonal. Compensatory hyperplasia allows for the regeneration of tissues and organs and is commonly observed in epithelial cells of the skin and intestines, liver cells (hepatocytes), bone marrow cells, and fibroblasts. It also occurs to a lesser extent in bone, cartilage, and smooth muscle cells. Hormonal hyperplasia typically occurs in organs that are dependent on estrogen. For instance, during pregnancy, uterine cells undergo both hyperplasia and hypertrophy in response to estrogen. Pathological hyperplasia, on the other hand, is an abnormal increase in cell division. A common example of pathological hyperplasia in women is endometrial hyperplasia, which is associated with a condition called endometriosis. Dysplasia refers to abnormal changes in the size, shape, and organization of cells. It is not considered a true form of cellular adaptation but is instead thought to be related to hyperplasia. Dysplasia is sometimes referred to as atypical hyperplasia. Tissues that are particularly susceptible to dysplasia include the epithelial cells of the cervix and respiratory tract. Dysplasia often occurs near cancerous cells and may play a role in the development of certain cancers, such as breast cancer. Metaplasia occurs when one type of differentiated cell is replaced by another type of cell, often one that is less specialized. This process is reversible and is believed to result from the reprogramming of stem cells. Stem cells are found in epithelial tissues and the embryonic mesenchyme of connective tissue. In this case, the normal mucus-secreting, ciliated columnar epithelial cells of the bronchial lining are replaced by non-ciliated, squamous epithelial cells that lack the ability to secrete mucus. If the irritant, such as cigarette smoke, is not removed, these metaplastic cells may progress to dysplasia or even become cancerous.
